snippet.title: How Many Eggs Should You Freeze? Real Numbers by Age
snippet.description:
How many eggs should you freeze? Dr Senai Aksoy, Associate Professor of Reproductive Medicine, walks through what the studies actually show: how your age at freezing and the total number of mature eggs shape your chance of having a baby later, why twice the eggs isn't twice the chance, and how the same logic works in IVF.

In short: your age at freezing sets the odds for each egg, and the total number of mature eggs decides how many tries you get at those odds. Freezing can improve your odds later, mostly when eggs are frozen younger, but it is not a guarantee of a baby.

CHAPTERS
00:00 How many eggs should I freeze?
01:07 Eggs, embryos and babies are not the same
02:05 The egg "talent show": from thaw to a normal embryo
03:14 How many eggs do you need at your age?
04:49 Does doubling your eggs double your chance?
05:56 IVF: same logic, different timing
06:47 Stimulation safety: a sensible number
07:12 Before you decide
07:59 My clinical view
08:32 Back to the dinner party
09:05 3 questions to ask your doctor

KEY NUMBERS
• Women who later used eggs frozen at 35 or younger: about 5 out of 10 had a baby. Frozen at 40 or older: about 2 out of 10 (2024 review).
• At one New York university clinic, with 20 or more mature eggs thawed: about 7–8 out of 10 women under 38, about 5 out of 10 at 38–40, and about 3–4 out of 10 at 41 or older had a baby or an ongoing pregnancy.
These are group averages from the studies below, not a personal forecast.

QUESTIONS TO ASK YOUR DOCTOR
1. How many mature eggs would you expect me to get per cycle, at my age and with my test results?
2. What's your lab's survival rate after thawing, and how many women my age have had a baby from their frozen eggs here?
3. If one cycle gives fewer eggs than we hoped, what would a second cycle realistically add?

SOURCES
• Hirsch et al., Human Reproduction Update 2024: live birth in women who returned to use eggs frozen for planned (elective) egg freezing, 10 studies, 1,517 women: https://doi.org/10.1093/humupd/dmae009
• Klein et al., Fertility and Sterility 2025: thawed mature eggs to chromosomally normal embryos, and how many women came back: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fertnstert.2025.12.003
• Cascante et al., Journal of Assisted Reproduction and Genetics 2024: age, mature eggs thawed and number of freezing cycles (NYU, 731 women): https://doi.org/10.1007/s10815-024-03175-w
• Sunkara et al., Human Reproduction 2011: eggs collected and predicted live birth after a fresh IVF cycle (UK, 400,135 cycles): https://doi.org/10.1093/humrep/der106
• Polyzos et al., Fertility and Sterility 2018: cumulative live birth (fresh and frozen embryos) by number of eggs: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fertnstert.2018.04.039
• Steward et al., Fertility and Sterility 2014: number of eggs and the risk of ovarian hyperstimulation: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fertnstert.2013.12.026
• ASRM Practice Committee 2021: outcomes after egg freezing, including outcomes of babies at birth: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fertnstert.2021.02.024

What would you like to ask about egg freezing or IVF numbers? Leave a question in the comments without sharing private medical details. Subscribe to Dr. Aksoy — Fertility, No Hype for clear explanations to help you prepare for discussions with your own doctor.

This video is for education and information only. It is not personal medical advice, a diagnosis or a treatment recommendation. Your individual circumstances require assessment by a qualified clinician. Do not make decisions about egg freezing, IVF or any treatment based on this video without consulting your doctor.
